scenes.text: So, where does Australia rank among wealthy countries? First, a puzzle. Country A spends far more per person on health than Country B, yet its people live shorter lives. Give three explanations that could each be true, without either country's data being wrong. Then pick the one you'd check first. Hold onto them, because the answer depends on what you compare, and how.

Whether a country's health is good is always a comparison. Compare Australia with a poor country, and you mostly learn about wealth. So we compare with the OECD, a group of mostly high-income countries that collect health data on agreed definitions. That holds wealth roughly steady, so the differences left point at choices: how the system is designed, what's spent on prevention, what's regulated. The most useful indicator is avoidable mortality: deaths that prevention or timely care could have stopped, because it shows what a system can influence. And three cautions. Rankings jump around, because many countries sit very close together. A national average can hide big gaps. And countries count differently. A difference in the data can be a difference in the counting.

So where does Australia sit? Think groups, not rank numbers, because rank numbers move. Australia is in the leading group for life expectancy, for males and females. It does better than average on avoidable deaths. Its daily smoking rate is among the lowest, and its cancer survival among the better. But it's average or weaker on others. Overweight and obesity are above average, and have risen for decades. Alcohol use sits around average or above. And, as in most OECD countries, only a small share of spending goes to prevention. Out-of-pocket costs, what patients pay themselves, are higher than in several similar countries, and heaviest for dental care. And there are big gaps inside the country. Put both columns together: healthy on average, and unevenly so.

Why? Sort explanations into three families. System: universal coverage through Medicare means cost is less often a barrier to seeing a GP, strong general practice catches problems early, and subsidised medicines keep long-term treatment affordable. Behaviour and policy: decades of tobacco control, with ad bans, taxes, plain packaging and smoke-free places, produced the low smoking rate, and fewer heart and cancer deaths follow. Population and environment: a younger population than many European and East Asian countries, and many migrants who arrive healthy. Now match the family to the indicator. Obesity, which raises heart disease and diabetes risk, isn't mainly a system failure. It comes from food environments, marketing and car-dependent suburbs, which is why clinics alone haven't shifted it. And high out-of-pocket costs are a system design outcome. They show up as delayed dental care, not delayed GP visits.

And why do some countries rank above or below us? Four variables explain most of the spread. One, whether coverage is universal. Where many people face cost as a barrier, avoidable deaths stay high, however advanced the hospitals. That answers the puzzle: the spending is real, but it isn't reaching everyone. Other answers could be an older population, or different counting. Two, how much goes to primary care and prevention, which act earlier in a disease. Three, income inequality and social spending, because health is made largely outside the health system. Four, long-standing patterns of diet, smoking and drinking, and the policies that shape them. And one idea explains many paradoxes: today's deaths reflect yesterday's exposures. A country that cut smoking thirty years ago is collecting the benefit now.

The last question is what we can learn and apply here. That needs a transfer test. Don't ask what another country does. Ask what makes it work, and whether that thing exists here. Step one, name the mechanism. Step two, check it against Australia: how spread out we are, our tax base, where our health workers live, and what's already covered. If the mechanism exists here, the policy transfers, with adaptations. If it doesn't, only the principle transfers, and you find a local way to carry it. So what passes? Sustained regulation, which worked for tobacco, applied to food marketing. Shifting spending toward prevention and primary care. And reporting by group, not just nationally. What fails? Anything that relies on dense cities, or on health workers spread evenly.
Two things to remember. Healthy on average, and unevenly so. And ask what makes it work, not what they do.

Two exam questions. First. Country C has fewer heart disease deaths than Australia today, but its obesity rate has risen sharply over the past fifteen years. A student predicts Country C will keep its lead. Assess this prediction. Pause here to answer.

The prediction is doubtful. Today's death rates reflect exposures from decades ago, so Country C's lead shows its past, not its future. Rising obesity raises diabetes and heart disease risk, and those deaths may arrive over the next twenty years. So its lead could narrow, unless treatment or prevention improves. The classic mistake is reading today's ranking as tomorrow's.

Second. Another OECD country cut childhood tooth decay with free dental care for everyone under eighteen, delivered in clinics at schools. Use the transfer test to judge whether it would work in Australia. Pause here to answer.

The mechanism: free care where children already are, so cost and travel stop being barriers. Some of it exists here already: schools reach almost every child, and some children already get subsidised dental care. But it strains in remote areas, with few dentists. So it transfers, adapted: widen what exists, with mobile and visiting teams for remote schools. The classic mistake is copying the policy without checking its mechanism.

So describe Australia by groups, not ranks, explain with at least two families, and only transfer a mechanism that exists here. Now take Australia's own bar, and split its deaths by cause. Two lines tell very different stories. Why are cardiovascular deaths falling while so many still live with it?
